games.title: Renegade
games.note: The Western version of Nekketsu Kōha Kunio-kun; it introduced the belt-scrolling brawler.

games.title: Double Dragon
games.note: Its name is a homage to Bruce Lee's Enter the Dragon; its success set off a flood of beat 'em ups.

games.title: Double Dragon II: The Revenge
games.note: The arcade version swapped punch and kick buttons for attack-left and attack-right buttons.

games.title: Final Fight
games.note: Mayor Mike Haggar's look came from the manga Mad Bull 34; it was first shown as Street Fighter '89.

games.title: Golden Axe
games.note: Players ride beasts and kick tiny thieves to steal their magic potions.

games.title: Altered Beast
games.note: Its hero turns into a werewolf and other beasts after collecting power-ups; it came packed in with early Mega Drives.

games.title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (arcade)
games.note: A four-player cabinet where each player took a different Turtle.

games.title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Turtles in Time
games.note: The SNES version let players hurl Foot soldiers at the screen.

games.title: Battletoads
games.note: Infamous for its Turbo Tunnel speeder-bike stage.

games.title: River City Ransom
games.note: Part of the Kunio-kun series; players spend dropped money in shops to raise their stats.

games.title: Guardian Heroes
games.note: A Saturn brawler with branching story paths and character levels.

games.title: Castle Crashers
games.note: Four-player co-op knights drawn by Dan Paladin, with levelling and animal companions.

games.title: Scott Pilgrim vs. the World: The Game
games.note: Paul Robertson led its pixel art and animation; Anamanaguchi wrote the chiptune soundtrack.

games.title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder's Revenge
games.note: Up to six players brawl together in the style of the 1987 cartoon.

games.title: Streets of Rage 4
games.note: Guard Crush Games built it on a modified version of the engine from its own Streets of Fury.

games.title: Fighting Force
games.note: A 3D brawler from Core Design, the studio behind Tomb Raider.

games.title: Cosmic Encounter
games.note: Each player is an alien race with a power that breaks the rules in its own way.

games.title: Magic: The Gathering
games.note: Designed by mathematician Richard Garfield; it started the collectible card game craze of the mid-1990s.

games.title: Magic: The Gathering Online
games.dev: Leaping Lizard Software / Wizards of the Coast
games.note: An online client where players buy, trade and play digital versions of Magic cards.

games.title: Magic: The Gathering Arena
games.note: Officially launched in 2019 after an open beta that began in 2018.

games.title: World of Warcraft Trading Card Game
games.note: Rare loot cards carried codes for items in World of Warcraft itself.

games.title: Gwent: The Witcher Card Game
games.note: Named after a card game from Andrzej Sapkowski's Witcher novels; matches are best of three rounds.

games.title: Legends of Runeterra
games.note: Riot's card game set in the League of Legends universe, launched with no card packs for sale.

games.title: Marvel Snap
games.note: Matches last about three minutes; Brode credits co-founder Hamilton Chu with the 'snap' that doubles the stakes.

games.title: Yu-Gi-Oh! Trading Card Game
games.note: Based on Kazuki Takahashi's manga, where the card game was first called Magic & Wizards.

games.title: Yu-Gi-Oh! Master Duel
games.note: A free-to-play digital version of the full card game with ranked online duels.

games.title: Pokémon Trading Card Game
games.note: The physical card game, launched in Japan in October 1996, months after Pokémon Red and Green.

games.title: Pokémon Trading Card Game (Game Boy)
games.note: Released in Japan as Pokémon Card GB; about 1.5 million copies sold in North America in its first year.

links.took: Kung-Fu Master laid the foundations for side-scrolling beat 'em ups.
links.added: Belt-scrolling: moving up and down the screen as well as sideways, against street gangs.

links.took: Kishimoto first planned it as a Kunio-kun (Renegade) game, keeping its brawling style.
links.added: Two-player co-op, weapons to pick up and a ruined city inspired by Mad Max.
links.extra: Wikipedia calls it Technōs Japan's spiritual successor to Kunio-kun.

links.took: The Kunio-kun series' street brawling and its hero Kunio.
links.added: A town to roam freely, shops that sell stat boosts, and passwords to save progress.
links.extra: Renegade was the Western version of the first Kunio-kun game.

links.took: Billy and Jimmy Lee's two-player street brawling.
links.added: Attack-left and attack-right buttons and a darker revenge story.

links.took: Producer Yoshiki Okamoto cited Double Dragon II as his basis for Final Fight.
links.added: Huge, detailed sprites, a wrestling mayor and Metro City's crime gang.
links.extra: Its title also changed following the success of Technōs Japan's Double Dragon.

links.took: Capcom first promoted it as a Street Fighter sequel called Street Fighter '89.
links.added: A side-scrolling brawler with three heroes instead of one-on-one fights.
links.extra: Arcade operators said it was nothing like Street Fighter, so the name changed.

links.took: Double Dragon's brawling: Makoto Uchida wanted 'a Double Dragon that was not a Double Dragon'.
links.added: A sword-and-sorcery world, magic spells and beasts to ride.

links.took: Street Fighter's mix of button presses and stick movements for individual attacks, per Uchida.
links.added: Those stick-and-button attack combinations in a fantasy brawler with magic.

links.took: Its fantasy world: Uchida felt arcade games should compete with the console hit Dragon Quest.
links.added: Swords, magic and a dwarf hero in fast arcade brawling instead of turn-based battles.
links.extra: Uchida studied 'the world of magic and swords' and combined it with Double Dragon's play.

links.took: Creator Makoto Uchida's previous brawler; a cockatrice-like beast appears in both games.
links.added: Three heroes with distinct styles, magic and rideable beasts.

links.took: Final Fight's street brawling: designer Noriyoshi Oba proposed a game along its lines.
links.added: Yuzo Koshiro's club-music soundtrack and a police car that fires a special attack.
links.extra: The Beat 'em up article says Streets of Rage borrowed heavily from Final Fight.

links.took: Double Dragon's co-op street fighting, which Oba named alongside Final Fight.
links.added: A home brawler for the Mega Drive with a techno soundtrack and three heroes.

links.took: Konami's four-player Turtles brawling.
links.added: Time-travel stages, from prehistory to the future.

links.took: A team of animal heroes, made in response to the Turtles craze.
links.added: Huge cartoon finishing hits, vehicle stages and punishing platforming.
links.extra: Wikipedia says Tim and Chris Stamper made it in response to the TMNT craze, not this game specifically.

links.took: Fantasy hack-and-slash brawling with magic, one of the beat 'em ups Tom Fulp named.
links.added: Four-player co-op, levelling up and animal companions with powers.

links.took: Side-scrolling co-op brawling against waves of enemies, one of Tom Fulp's named influences.
links.added: Cartoon knights, magic attacks and RPG-style stats.

links.took: Character levels and stats in a co-op brawler, from one of Fulp's named influences.
links.added: Cartoon humour, unlockable knights and animal orb companions.

links.took: Its chunky cartoon look: Dan Paladin's primary inspiration for the art style.
links.added: Paladin's hand-drawn knights and four-player co-op.

links.took: River City Ransom's open brawling and stat-boosting shops; the game references it directly.
links.added: Paul Robertson's pixel art, Anamanaguchi's chiptune score and the comics' cast.

src.t: Wikipedia: Scott Pilgrim vs. the World: The Game

links.extra: Wikipedia lists River City Ransom among the games it references.

links.took: Turtles in Time's arcade brawling and look, which inspired the game.
links.added: Six-player co-op, a story mode with upgrades, and new playable characters.

src.t: Wikipedia: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder's Revenge

links.extra: It was also inspired by the 1987 animated series.

links.took: The style of Konami's arcade Turtles brawlers from the 1980s and 1990s.
links.added: Up to six players, Tribute Games' pixel art and characters like April and Splinter.

src.t: Wikipedia: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder's Revenge

links.took: Elements of Battletoads, per Wikipedia; the source doesn't say which.
links.added: A Turtles brawler for up to six players with a cartoon-faithful look.

src.t: Wikipedia: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder's Revenge

links.took: Streets of Rage's fighters, such as Axel and Blaze, and its co-op brawling.
links.added: Lizardcube's hand-drawn art, combo-focused fighting and new characters.
links.extra: Streets of Rage 3 came in between; players can switch to the first two games' soundtracks.

links.took: It began as Core Design's planned Streets of Rage sequel for the Saturn.
links.added: 3D streets, objects to smash or wield as weapons, and four new heroes.
links.extra: Sega pulled the Streets of Rage name, so it came out as Fighting Force.

links.took: Rule-breaking powers: Richard Garfield called Cosmic Encounter Magic's most influential ancestor.
links.added: Collectible cards that each bend the rules, and decks players build themselves.

src.t: Richard Garfield, 'The Creation of Magic: The Gathering' (1993), Wizards of the Coast

links.extra: Garfield first tried to distill Cosmic Encounter's modularity into a card game called Five Magics in 1982.

links.took: Magic's cards and rules.
links.added: Online play and card trading on PC, built with help from Leaping Lizard.

links.took: Digital Magic for online play.
links.added: A modern free-to-play client with faster, automated play.

links.took: Hearthstone's format: Wizards planned to adapt Magic 'into a digital format similar to Hearthstone'.
links.added: Magic's full rules and card sets, with free-to-play progression.

links.took: Magic popularized collectible card battles: decks, resources each turn and summoned creatures.
links.added: Faster play: automatic mana, no responses on the opponent's turn, and hero powers.
links.extra: Wikipedia notes that, unlike Magic, Hearthstone was designed to speed up play.

links.took: Magic popularized the collectible card game format.
links.added: World of Warcraft heroes, raid decks, and loot cards with codes for in-game items.

links.took: World of Warcraft's heroes, classes and art.
links.added: A physical card game with hero cards and raid decks.

links.took: Concepts and art: Hearthstone's team drew ideas and art from the WoW card game.
links.added: A digital-only design with automatic rules, fast turns and free-to-play packs.
links.extra: Blizzard ended the physical game's licence with Cryptozoic in favour of Hearthstone.

links.took: Hearthstone's success, which encouraged its release as a standalone digital card game.
links.added: Best-of-three rounds on a row-based board, and bluffing over when to pass.

links.took: The card minigame players met in The Witcher 3's taverns.
links.added: A standalone online game with ranked play and new factions.

src.t: Wikipedia: Gwent: The Witcher Card Game

links.took: Magic's collectible card design; Wikipedia says Runeterra was inspired by it.
links.added: Alternating attack turns, champions that level up, and no paid card packs.
links.extra: Riot's balancing director named two lead designers as big Magic fans.

links.took: League of Legends' world and champions.
links.added: A collectible card game set in Runeterra.

links.took: Hearthstone popularized free-to-play digital card games built for online play.
links.added: Turns where the opponent can respond with spells, and generous free card unlocks.
links.extra: Wikipedia says Hearthstone's success led to a number of similar digital-only card games.

links.took: Ben Brode said he was directly inspired by his experiences working on Hearthstone.
links.added: Three-minute matches, simultaneous turns, three locations and the 'snap' to double the stakes.
links.extra: Brode and Hamilton Chu, former Hearthstone leaders, founded Second Dinner to make it.

links.took: Brode also named his work on the World of Warcraft Trading Card Game as a direct inspiration.
links.added: A much quicker card game with a lower barrier to entry, set in the Marvel universe.

links.took: Magic popularized collectible card duels.
links.added: Monster, spell and trap cards from a hit manga, with life points and no mana.
links.extra: The manga's card game was first called 'Magic & Wizards'.

links.took: The full Yu-Gi-Oh! card game and its card pool.
links.added: Free-to-play online duels with automated rules.

links.took: Magic popularized collectible card battles.
links.added: Pokémon that evolve and attack using energy cards, aimed at younger players.

links.took: Pokémon's creatures, types and evolutions.
links.added: A physical card game powered by energy cards.

links.took: The tabletop game's rules and cards from its first three sets.
links.added: Computer opponents to duel, and cards found only in the Game Boy game.

src.t: Wikipedia: Pokémon Trading Card Game (video game)
